memoryText: Know that the LORD, he is God! It is he who made us, and we are his; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Psalm 100:3 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
After a week of reading about rebellion, judgment, and the long wandering of the wilderness generation, Psalm 100:3 is a place to rest. It tells you who God is, and who you are.

“Know that the LORD, he is God.” The verse begins with an instruction to know. Knowledge here is more than information. It is acknowledgment, the settled recognition of who is God and who is not. Much of Israel’s trouble in the wilderness came from forgetting this.

“It is he who made us, and we are his.” Two ideas come together: creation and belonging. God made us, so we depend on him for life. And we are his, so we are cared for. We do not have to prove ourselves or earn a place. Our identity rests on his making and his claim.

“We are his people.” The phrase comes from the covenant: “I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God” (Exodus 6:7). It is a corporate identity, not only a private one. We belong to a people.

“And the sheep of his pasture.” Sheep are helpless and prone to wander. A shepherd leads them to food and water, protects them from wolves, and finds them when they are lost. The image describes how God treated Israel in the wilderness, even when they did not deserve it.

For the Christian, the verse finds its full meaning in Jesus, the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). He knows his own and calls them by name, and no one can snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28).
weekInReview: This week you followed Israel through more of the wilderness. You read the laws that look ahead to the land, and the rebellion of Korah, which was answered by the earth opening and by Aaron standing between the living and the dead. You saw Aaron’s staff bud, learned that the priests have God himself as their inheritance, and read the puzzling law of the red heifer. You read of Moses’ failure at the rock, the death of Miriam and Aaron, and the bronze serpent that healed all who looked. You heard the story of Balaam, the prophet who could only bless, and the prophecy of the star out of Jacob. In the Psalms, you read Psalm 99, which holds God’s forgiveness and holiness together, and Psalm 100, a song of thanks. The week taught that God preserves his plan despite human failure, and that his chosen mediator saves.
reflectionQuestions: Aaron stood between the living and the dead with a censer of incense, and the plague stopped. How does this picture help you understand what Jesus does for you?
The people were healed by looking at the bronze serpent. What does this story teach you about how faith works, and what do you need to look at today?
Psalm 100 says, “It is he who made us, and we are his.” How would it change your week to remember that you belong to God?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he made you and that you are his.
Thank Jesus, the good shepherd who lays down his life.
